t: Employees Whose Manager Left the Company — Anti-Join Against Missing Managers
o: Report employees earning strictly under $30000 whose manager_id still points at a person who no longer exists in the Employees table. Rows with NULL manager_id have no manager at all and must be excluded. Walking the sample: Mila fails the salary filter; Antonella and Emery have NULL managers; Kalel earns 21241 but his manager 11 (Joziah) is still employed; Joziah himself earns 28485 and his manager 6 is gone, so employee_id 11 is the only output row, ordered by employee_id. Structurally this is an anti-join: keep rows whose manager_id matches no existing employee_id.
k: Two filters combine: salary < 30000 AND manager_id referencing a deleted employee.
manager_id IS NOT NULL must be stated explicitly — NULL never matches anything, yet in LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL patterns unfiltered NULL rows sneak through.
Anti-joins are expressible both as NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL; MySQL plans them identically.

a.i: Select under-$30000 employees for whom no live employee shares their manager_id. This states the intent directly and handles NULL manager_ids gracefully, since a NULL simply finds no match and the explicit IS NOT NULL guard keeps semantics clean.
s: Reject rows where an employee with id equal to manager_id exists.
Order the surviving ids by employee_id.

c.python:
-- Database problem — the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
SELECT e.employee_id
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary < 30000
  AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM Employees m
      WHERE m.employee_id = e.manager_id
  )
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

a.n: Approach 2: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL Anti-Join
a.i: Join each employee to the (hypothetical) row of their manager; unmatched joins leave NULLs on the right side, so demanding e2.employee_id IS NULL retains exactly the orphaned reports. A classic pre-window-function idiom that reads well once recognized.
s: LEFT JOIN Employees to itself on manager_id = employee_id.
Keep rows where the joined manager side is entirely NULL.
Apply the salary filter and the non-null manager guard.

c.python:
-- Database problem — the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
SELECT e1.employee_id
FROM Employees e1
LEFT JOIN Employees e2
       ON e1.manager_id = e2.employee_id
WHERE e1.salary < 30000
  AND e1.manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND e2.employee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY e1.employee_id;

w: Either formulation passes; say out loud why the NULL guard matters — that is the trap the problem is built around. Pitfalls: dropping manager_id IS NOT NULL (NULL-manager rows leak into the LEFT JOIN result), using INNER JOIN (it silently discards precisely the orphaned rows you need), and omitting ORDER BY when the grader compares ordered output. Follow-up: delete orphaned reports in cascade, or list employees whose entire management chain above them is gone (recursive CTE).
